title: Sizing the platform
outcome: Leadership asks how big a shared Kafka platform must be, and the first estimate forgot replication and the consumers.

content.bookmark: Disk = data per day × retention days × replication factor. Network out = data in × consumer groups, plus replication. Partitions come from measured throughput and needed parallelism, with headroom.

check.prompt: 0.5 TB of data a day, 7 days of retention, replication factor 3. How much disk does the data need across the cluster?
check.why: 0.5 × 7 = 3.5 TB for one copy, × 3 replicas = 10.5 TB, before headroom.

check.prompt: 20 MB/s is produced, with replication factor 3 and 4 consumer groups reading everything. Roughly how much leaves the brokers?
options: About 80 MB/s to consumers plus 40 MB/s of replication to followers
check.why: Each group reads the full 20 MB/s, and two followers each copy it once. Network often runs out before disk.

check.prompt: How many controllers do the KRaft docs typically recommend, and why?
options: 3 or 5: a majority must be alive, so 3 tolerate one failure and 5 tolerate two
check.why: The metadata quorum needs a majority. Combined broker-and-controller servers are not recommended for critical deployments.

check.prompt: Why decide partition counts up front, with headroom?
options: Consumers can't read more than 10 partitions
Partitions can't be reduced, and adding them later moves keys
check.why: Changing the count later is disruptive for ordered topics, and you can never go down.

caseStudy.setting: A bank (fictional) is consolidating five teams' event streams onto one shared Kafka platform. Leadership asks for a size and a cost. Inputs: peak 40 MB/s in, about 1 TB a day, 7 days of retention, replication factor 3, and each event read by 3 consumer groups on average.

events.what: A first estimate says 7 TB of disk and 3 brokers: 1 TB a day for 7 days.
Architecture review asks about replicas, consumer traffic, a broker failure and controllers. The estimate has none of them.
Leadership needs a defensible number by Friday, with the assumptions stated.

pipeline: 5 teams · producers, peak 40 MB/s in total
Topics · replication factor 3, min ISR 2, 7 days of retention
3 consumer groups per event on average
Cluster · brokers and KRaft controllers to be sized
tasks: What did the first estimate leave out?
Work out disk, network and the shape of the cluster.

debrief.title: What was missing
text: Replication: every byte is stored three times. 1 TB × 7 days × 3 = 21 TB, not 7.
Headroom: room to grow, and to re-copy a failed broker's data onto the others. Keeping disks around half full, a common planning choice rather than a Kafka rule, means about 42 TB of raw disk.
Consumers and replication on the network: at peak 40 MB/s in, 80 MB/s of follower replication, and 120 MB/s to three consumer groups.

debrief.title: The shape of the cluster
text: Brokers: divide disk and network by what one broker can carry on your hardware, keep at least 3 for replication factor 3, and add one so the cluster still holds the load with a broker down.
Controllers: 3 dedicated KRaft controllers, so the metadata quorum survives one failure. Combined servers suit development, not critical systems.
Partitions per topic: from measured per-partition throughput and needed consumer parallelism, the larger, with headroom.

debrief.title: What to measure before committing
text: Per-partition throughput with real record sizes and compression; consumer processing rates; recovery time after a broker loss.
If retention is the main driver of disk, tiered storage can move older segments off broker disks, with a remote storage plugin and its limits.

takeaway: Disk is data × retention × replicas, plus headroom.
Network out is consumers plus replication, and often the real limit.
State the assumptions, measure, and plan for losing a broker.
content.honesty: If you haven't sized a cluster, say so and do the arithmetic out loud with stated assumptions. If you have, lead with the number that turned out wrong.

tasks: What inputs would you get from the five teams?
What would you include in the platform's service level?

debrief.title: Inputs
text: Peak and average volume, record size, retention need, how many consumers, and growth over two years, per team.

debrief.title: Service level
text: Durability (replication factor 3, min ISR 2), availability with one broker down, and lag targets per consumer.

sayIt.question: How would you gather requirements for a shared streaming platform?
points: Volumes at peak and average, record sizes, growth.
Retention needs from each team's replay requirements.
Number of consumers per stream.
Durability and availability expectations.
Owners and change process per team.

tasks: How do you present the number to leadership?
How do you allocate cost across teams?

debrief.title: Presenting
text: Show the formula, the assumptions and a range, and what would change it: retention, consumers, growth.

debrief.title: Allocating cost
text: By each team's bytes in × retention × replicas, plus consumer traffic, so teams see the cost of their choices.

sayIt.question: How would you justify the size and cost of a shared Kafka platform?
points: Show the drivers: volume, retention, replication, consumers.
State assumptions and give a range.
Include headroom for failure and growth.
Allocate cost by usage so choices have visible cost.
Revisit with real measurements.

tasks: How do you plan the rollout?
What capacity process do you set up?

debrief.title: Rollout
text: Onboard one team at a time, measuring real throughput and lag before the next.

debrief.title: Capacity process
text: Quarterly capacity review against disk, network and partition counts; onboarding requests include volumes and retention.

sayIt.question: How would you roll out a shared platform to several teams?
points: Onboard in stages, measuring as you go.
Require volumes and retention with each request.
Review capacity regularly.
Keep headroom for a broker loss.
Communicate limits and costs.

debrief.title: Arithmetic
text: Disk: 1 TB/day × 7 × 3 = 21 TB, about 42 TB raw at half full.
Network at peak: 40 in, 80 replication, 120 out, so about 200 MB/s leaving brokers in total.

debrief.title: Benchmarks
text: kafka-producer-perf-test and kafka-consumer-perf-test with real record sizes, acks=all and compression on, on the target hardware; then a broker-loss test while loaded.

sayIt.question: Walk me through sizing a Kafka cluster.
points: Disk: data per day × retention × replication factor, plus headroom.
Network: in, plus replication, plus each consumer group.
Partitions: the larger of throughput need and parallelism need, with headroom.
Brokers: enough for disk and network, at least 3, plus one spare; 3 or 5 KRaft controllers.
Measure on real hardware and test a broker loss.
